authors: Schwarz, N., & Clore, G. L.
title: Mood, misattribution, and judgments of well-being: Informative and directive functions of affective states
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 45(3), 513–523
finding: People in a good mood (including people phoned on sunny days) rated their happiness and life satisfaction higher. A bad mood stopped lowering their ratings once their attention was drawn to an outside cause, such as the weather.
strength: moderate: a classic demonstration of "feelings as information"; later large studies found the weather effect on life satisfaction to be very small.
verified_by: https://worlddatabaseofhappiness.eur.nl/publications/mood-misattribution-and-judgements-of-well-being-informative-and-directive-functions-of-affective-states-1841 ; https://api.isr.umich.edu/?p=190605 (DOI not confirmed in search, so none given)

authors: James, W.
title: What is an emotion?
finding: James argued that bodily changes follow directly from perceiving something exciting, and that our feeling of those bodily changes is the emotion.
strength: debated: a founding theory; challenged by Cannon and others, but body–feeling links remain central in emotion science.

authors: Schachter, S., & Singer, J.
title: Cognitive, social, and physiological determinants of emotional state
finding: Proposed the two-factor theory: an emotion is physical arousal plus a label we give it from the situation.
strength: debated: the original experiment has not replicated well, though the broad idea is still influential.

authors: Craig, A. D.
title: How do you feel? Interoception: the sense of the physiological condition of the body
finding: Described a pathway that carries signals about the body's internal state to the brain (including the insula), and proposed it underlies subjective feelings, emotion and self-awareness.
strength: strong: a foundational, widely cited review; some proposals remain theoretical.

authors: Barrett, L. F.
title: The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization
finding: Sets out the theory that the brain constantly predicts the body's needs and constructs emotions by making sense of body sensations using learned concepts.
strength: debated: influential and actively tested; basic-emotion researchers disagree.

authors: Lieberman, M. D., Eisenberger, N. I., Crockett, M. J., Tom, S. M., Pfeifer, J. H., & Way, B. M.
title: Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli
finding: In a brain-imaging study, labelling the emotion in a picture reduced amygdala and other limbic responses compared with other ways of processing the image.
strength: moderate: replicated lab finding; effects are modest and mostly measured with pictures in the lab.

authors: Torre, J. B., & Lieberman, M. D.
title: Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling as implicit emotion regulation
finding: Reviewed evidence that naming a feeling can reduce its intensity even though it does not feel like regulating it at the time.
strength: moderate: consistent lab evidence; the authors say understanding of how it works is still early.

authors: Kircanski, K., Lieberman, M. D., & Craske, M. G.
title: Feelings into words: Contributions of language to exposure therapy
finding: Spider-fearful people who described their feelings in words while near a live spider showed lower skin-conductance arousal a week later than people who reappraised, distracted themselves or had exposure alone; self-reported fear did not differ between groups.
strength: early: a single small experiment.

authors: Pennebaker, J. W., & Beall, S. K.
title: Confronting a traumatic event: Toward an understanding of inhibition and disease
finding: An early expressive-writing experiment in which students wrote about traumatic experiences over several days; it launched decades of research on whether writing about difficult experiences helps health and well-being.
strength: moderate: launched a large literature; later meta-analyses find small average benefits.

authors: Frattaroli, J.
title: Experimental disclosure and its moderators: A meta-analysis
finding: Pooling 146 randomized studies, experimental disclosure (such as expressive writing) had a small but significant positive average effect.
strength: moderate: real but small effect that varies by person and outcome.

authors: Kashdan, T. B., Barrett, L. F., & McKnight, P. E.
title: Unpacking emotion differentiation: Transforming unpleasant experience by perceiving distinctions in negativity
finding: Reviewed research on emotion differentiation (emotional granularity): people who describe negative feelings in fine-grained ways tend to rely less on unhelpful coping such as binge drinking or aggression.
strength: moderate: consistent findings, but mostly correlational.

authors: Wegner, D. M., Schneider, D. J., Carter, S. R., & White, T. L.
title: Paradoxical effects of thought suppression
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 53(1), 5–13
finding: People asked not to think of a white bear kept thinking of it, suggesting that trying to suppress a thought can backfire.
strength: moderate: classic, widely replicated in broad form; size of the rebound varies.

authors: Verduyn, P., & Lavrijsen, S.
title: Which emotions last longest and why: The role of event importance and rumination
finding: Of 27 emotions studied, sadness lasted longest, while shame, surprise, fear and disgust were among the shortest; long-lasting emotions tended to follow important events and involve rumination.
strength: moderate: a single self-report study, consistent with other duration research.

authors: Hatfield, E., Cacioppo, J. T., & Rapson, R. L.
title: Emotional contagion
venue: Cambridge University Press (Studies in Emotion and Social Interaction)
finding: Describes emotional contagion: people tend to mimic each other's faces, voices and postures, and that mimicry can shift their own feelings.
strength: moderate: well supported face to face; online contagion effects are small.

authors: Gross, J. J.
title: The emerging field of emotion regulation: An integrative review
finding: Set out the process model of emotion regulation, with five points where emotion can be shaped: situation selection, situation modification, attention, cognitive change (reappraisal) and response modulation.
strength: strong: the dominant framework in emotion-regulation research.

authors: Gross, J. J., & John, O. P.
title: Individual differences in two emotion regulation processes: Implications for affect, relationships, and well-being
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 85(2), 348–362
finding: Across five studies, people who habitually reappraised had better emotional experience, relationships and well-being; habitual suppression was linked to worse outcomes.
strength: strong: widely replicated, though costs of suppression vary across cultures.

authors: Butler, E. A., Egloff, B., Wilhelm, F. H., Smith, N. C., Erickson, E. A., & Gross, J. J.
title: The social consequences of expressive suppression
finding: When one person hid their emotions while discussing an upsetting topic, communication suffered, their partner's blood pressure rose, and rapport and relationship formation were reduced.
strength: moderate: two lab studies with unacquainted women.

authors: Bushman, B. J.
title: Does venting anger feed or extinguish the flame? Catharsis, rumination, distraction, anger, and aggressive responding
finding: Angered people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who provoked them felt angrier afterwards than people who were distracted or did nothing.
strength: moderate: a single experiment, consistent with later meta-analytic work.

authors: Kjærvik, S. L., & Bushman, B. J.
title: A meta-analytic review of anger management activities that increase or decrease arousal: What fuels or douses rage?
finding: Across 154 studies, activities that calm the body (such as slow breathing, relaxation and mindfulness) reduced anger and aggression, while arousal-increasing activities showed little or no benefit.
strength: moderate: a large meta-analysis; the authors say more research is needed. DOI not confirmed in search, so the link is the university news release.

authors: Sifneos, P. E.
title: The prevalence of "alexithymic" characteristics in psychosomatic patients
finding: Introduced the term "alexithymia" for difficulty finding words for feelings, along with a limited fantasy life, and found these traits more often in psychosomatic patients than in controls.
strength: early: small clinical sample; historically important as the origin of the term.

authors: Bagby, R. M., Parker, J. D. A., & Taylor, G. J.
title: The twenty-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale—I. Item selection and cross-validation of the factor structure
finding: Developed the 20-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20) and tested its three-factor structure in clinical and non-clinical groups.
strength: strong: the most widely used alexithymia measure, though self-report has limits.

authors: Kinnaird, E., Stewart, C., & Tchanturia, K.
title: Investigating alexithymia in autism: A systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Across 15 studies, about half of autistic participants (around 50%) had high alexithymia compared with about 5% of comparison participants; alexithymia is common in autism but not universal.
strength: moderate: consistent across studies, but based mostly on self-report questionnaires.

authors: Bird, G., & Cook, R.
title: Mixed emotions: The contribution of alexithymia to the emotional symptoms of autism
finding: Argued that emotional difficulties seen in some autistic people are better explained by co-occurring alexithymia than by autism itself.
strength: moderate: an influential hypothesis with growing support; still being tested.

authors: Tangney, J. P., & Dearing, R. L.
title: Shame and guilt
finding: Summarizes years of research distinguishing shame (about the self) from guilt (about the act): guilt-proneness goes with empathy and repair, shame-proneness with hiding, blame and anger.
strength: moderate: a large body of research, with some debate about whether measures fully separate the two and about cultural differences.

authors: Lewis, H. B.
title: Shame and guilt in neurosis
finding: Drawing on therapy sessions, Lewis distinguished shame, which centres on the whole self, from guilt, which centres on a specific act.
strength: moderate: clinical observation that later research by Tangney and others built on.

authors: Nolen-Hoeksema, S.
title: Responses to depression and their effects on the duration of depressive episodes
finding: Proposed the response styles theory: people who ruminate on their low mood tend to have longer depressions than people who distract themselves.
strength: strong: extensive, consistent later research.

authors: Rose, A. J.
title: Co-rumination in the friendships of girls and boys
finding: In 608 school students, co-rumination (repeatedly going over problems with a friend) was linked both to closer friendships and to more depression and anxiety symptoms; girls co-ruminated more.
strength: moderate: replicated mostly with adolescents; correlational.

authors: Bonanno, G. A.
title: Loss, trauma, and human resilience: Have we underestimated the human capacity to thrive after extremely aversive events?
finding: Argued that resilience after loss or trauma is distinct from recovery, is more common than many theorists assumed, and can come about in several ways.
strength: strong: supported by many later trajectory studies.

authors: Masten, A. S.
title: Ordinary magic: Resilience processes in development
finding: Concluded that resilience is common and usually arises from ordinary human adaptive systems, such as relationships; the main threats are things that damage those systems.
strength: strong: influential review of developmental research.

authors: Fredrickson, B. L.
title: The role of positive emotions in positive psychology: The broaden-and-build theory of positive emotions
finding: Proposed that positive emotions broaden attention and thinking and, over time, help build lasting personal resources.
strength: moderate: influential, with experimental support for broadening; the separate "positivity ratio" claim was discredited.

authors: Brown, N. J. L., Sokal, A. D., & Friedman, H. L.
title: The complex dynamics of wishful thinking: The critical positivity ratio
finding: Showed that the mathematical model behind the claimed "critical positivity ratio" of 2.9013 had no valid basis, so the ratio claim was unfounded.
strength: strong: a decisive critique of one specific claim.

authors: Barrett, L. F., Adolphs, R., Marsella, S., Martinez, A. M., & Pollak, S. D.
title: Emotional expressions reconsidered: Challenges to inferring emotion from human facial movements
venue: Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 20(1), 1–68
finding: Concluded that facial movements are not reliable enough to infer a person's specific emotion across situations and cultures.
strength: debated: a major review; basic-emotion researchers dispute parts of it.

authors: Kramer, A. D. I., Guillory, J. E., & Hancock, J. T.
title: Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks
finding: Changing how many positive or negative posts Facebook users saw slightly shifted the emotional tone of their own posts.
strength: debated: very small effects, and the journal published an editorial expression of concern about consent.

authors: Eisenberger, N. I., Lieberman, M. D., & Williams, K. D.
title: Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion
finding: Being left out of a virtual ball-tossing game increased activity in the anterior cingulate cortex, a region also involved in physical pain distress, in proportion to how upset people felt.
strength: debated: influential small brain-imaging study; how closely social and physical pain overlap is still argued.

authors: Leary, M. R., Springer, C., Negel, L., Ansell, E., & Evans, K.
title: The causes, phenomenology, and consequences of hurt feelings
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1225–1237
finding: Hurt feelings were triggered by events that signalled relational devaluation (feeling less valued by someone), usually by people the person knew well.
strength: moderate: retrospective accounts; widely supported idea.

authors: Singer, T., & Klimecki, O. M.
title: Empathy and compassion
finding: Distinguished empathic distress (sharing someone's pain, which can overwhelm) from compassion (warm concern), which engage different brain networks; brief compassion training increased positive feelings.
strength: early: promising lab studies with relatively small samples.

authors: Figley, C. R. (Ed.)
title: Compassion fatigue: Coping with secondary traumatic stress disorder in those who treat the traumatized
finding: An edited volume introducing "compassion fatigue" as a cost of helping traumatized people, distinguished from burnout and PTSD, with ideas for prevention.
strength: moderate: a widely used clinical concept; measurement is debated.

authors: Taylor, S. E., Klein, L. C., Lewis, B. P., Gruenewald, T. L., Gurung, R. A. R., & Updegraff, J. A.
title: Biobehavioral responses to stress in females: Tend-and-befriend, not fight-or-flight
finding: Proposed that under stress people, perhaps especially women, often respond by protecting others and seeking social connection ("tend and befriend"), not only fight or flight.
strength: moderate: influential theory with supporting evidence; sex differences are debated.

authors: Lazarus, R. S., & Folkman, S.
title: Stress, appraisal, and coping
finding: Set out the appraisal model: stress depends on judging whether something threatens you and whether you can cope; it also distinguished problem-focused from emotion-focused coping.
strength: strong: one of the most influential frameworks in stress research.

authors: Grossman, P., & Taylor, E. W.
title: Toward understanding respiratory sinus arrhythmia: Relations to cardiac vagal tone, evolution and biobehavioral functions
finding: Raised caveats about using respiratory sinus arrhythmia as an index of vagal tone and challenged evolutionary assumptions used in polyvagal theory.
strength: strong: a detailed physiological critique.

authors: Grossman, P.
title: Fundamental challenges and likely refutations of the five basic premises of the polyvagal theory
finding: Reviewed the evidence for each of polyvagal theory's five basic premises and argued that each is untenable or highly implausible.
strength: debated: a strong critique; Porges and colleagues have responded.

authors: Arnsten, A. F. T.
title: Stress signalling pathways that impair prefrontal cortex structure and function
finding: Reviewed evidence that stress chemicals rapidly weaken the prefrontal cortex, which supports planning and flexible thinking, while strengthening more habitual responses.
strength: strong: well-established neuroscience, much of it from animal studies.

authors: McEwen, B. S., & Stellar, E.
title: Stress and the individual: Mechanisms leading to disease
finding: Introduced "allostatic load": the cumulative wear and tear on the body from repeated or chronic stress responses.
strength: moderate: a widely used framework; there is no single agreed way to measure it.

authors: McEwen, B. S.
title: Protective and damaging effects of stress mediators
finding: Explained how the same stress hormones that protect us in the short term cause wear and tear (allostatic load) when stress systems are chronically over- or under-active.
strength: strong: highly influential review.

authors: Kanner, A. D., Coyne, J. C., Schaefer, C., & Lazarus, R. S.
title: Comparison of two modes of stress measurement: Daily hassles and uplifts versus major life events
finding: Everyday hassles predicted psychological symptoms better than major life events did, and still did after life events were taken into account.
strength: moderate: a classic study; many later studies support the importance of daily hassles.

authors: Repetti, R. L.
title: Effects of daily workload on subsequent behavior during marital interaction: The roles of social withdrawal and spouse support
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 57(4), 651–659
finding: Air traffic controllers (33) and their wives reported over three days; after high-workload days the controllers were more socially withdrawn at home, especially when their wives were supportive.
strength: moderate: a small, influential daily study of stress spillover.

authors: Yoo, S.-S., Gujar, N., Hu, P., Jolesz, F. A., & Walker, M. P.
title: The human emotional brain without sleep—a prefrontal amygdala disconnect
finding: After a night without sleep, the amygdala reacted more strongly to negative pictures and was less connected to the prefrontal cortex.
strength: moderate: a small lab study, consistent with later sleep research.

authors: Gordon, A. M., & Chen, S.
title: The role of sleep in interpersonal conflict: Do sleepless nights mean worse fights?
finding: In a 14-day daily study, people reported more conflict with their partner after poor nights of sleep, and conflicts were resolved best when both partners were well rested.
strength: moderate: diary and lab evidence; correlational in part.

authors: Zaccaro, A., Piarulli, A., Laurino, M., Garbella, E., Menicucci, D., Neri, B., & Gemignani, A.
title: How breath-control can change your life: A systematic review on psycho-physiological correlates of slow breathing
finding: Slow breathing was linked with changes in heart-rate variability and with more comfort, relaxation and alertness and less arousal and anxiety.
strength: moderate: consistent direction, but many included studies were small.

authors: Balban, M. Y., Neri, E., Kogon, M. M., Weed, L., Nouriani, B., Jo, B., Holl, G., Zeitzer, J. M., Spiegel, D., & Huberman, A. D.
title: Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal
finding: In a month-long randomized trial of five minutes a day, breathing exercises improved mood more than mindfulness meditation, with cyclic sighing (long out-breaths) showing the largest benefits.
strength: early: a single remote trial; needs replication.

authors: Sonnentag, S., & Fritz, C.
title: The Recovery Experience Questionnaire: Development and validation of a measure for assessing recuperation and unwinding from work
finding: Identified four separate recovery experiences outside work: psychological detachment, relaxation, mastery and control.
strength: strong: widely used measure; recovery research is extensive and consistent.

authors: Leikas, S., & Ilmarinen, V.-J.
title: Happy now, tired later? Extraverted and conscientious behavior are related to immediate mood gains, but to later fatigue
finding: In a 12-day experience-sampling study, acting extraverted went with better mood at the time but more fatigue about three hours later, for introverts and extraverts alike.
strength: early: small sample (48 people); the authors called for replication.

authors: Coan, J. A., Schaefer, H. S., & Davidson, R. J.
title: Lending a hand: Social regulation of the neural response to threat
finding: Married women facing threat of a mild shock showed less threat-related brain activity when holding their husband's hand, more so in higher-quality marriages.
strength: early: a small study (16 women), but part of a consistent wider literature.

authors: Coan, J. A., & Sbarra, D. A.
title: Social baseline theory: The social regulation of risk and effort
finding: Proposes that the brain expects to have supportive people around, which lowers perceived risk and effort; without them, coping takes more effort.
strength: moderate: a theory supported by a growing set of mostly small studies.

authors: Butler, E. A., & Randall, A. K.
title: Emotional coregulation in close relationships
finding: Defined emotional coregulation as a two-way link between partners' emotional states that helps keep both of them steady.
strength: moderate: conceptual review of mostly small lab studies.

authors: Khalsa, S. S., Adolphs, R., Cameron, O. G., Critchley, H. D., Davenport, P. W., Feinstein, J. S., et al.
title: Interoception and mental health: A roadmap
venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging, 3(6), 501–513
finding: A consensus review from the 2016 Interoception Summit on how to measure interoception and study its role in mental health.
strength: moderate: expert consensus; the field is still developing reliable measures.

authors: Yerkes, R. M., & Dodson, J. D.
title: The relation of strength of stimulus to rapidity of habit-formation
venue: Journal of Comparative Neurology and Psychology, 18(5), 459–482
finding: Studied how the strength of an electric shock affected how quickly dancing mice learned to avoid a black passage; later writers turned it into a general "inverted U" for arousal and performance.
strength: debated: the original was an animal study; the popular human "law" is an oversimplification.

authors: Maslach, C., & Jackson, S. E.
title: The measurement of experienced burnout
finding: Introduced the Maslach Burnout Inventory, with three parts: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization and reduced personal accomplishment.
strength: strong: the standard burnout measure; its overlap with depression is debated.

authors: World Health Organization
title: Burn-out an "occupational phenomenon": International Classification of Diseases
finding: ICD-11 includes burn-out as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition: a syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, with exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism, and reduced professional efficacy.
strength: strong: official classification statement.

authors: Pinquart, M., & Sörensen, S.
title: Differences between caregivers and noncaregivers in psychological health and physical health: A meta-analysis
finding: Across 84 studies, caregivers reported more stress and depression and lower well-being than non-caregivers, with smaller differences in physical health and larger differences for dementia caregivers.
strength: strong: large meta-analysis; caregiving also brings positive aspects such as meaning.

authors: MacCormack, J. K., & Lindquist, K. A.
title: Feeling hangry? When hunger is conceptualized as emotion
finding: Hunger made people judge things more negatively in negative situations, and in the lab hungry people felt worse and judged a researcher more harshly, but mainly when they were not paying attention to their own feelings.
strength: early: a few experiments; the authors argue hunger alone is not enough to cause "hangriness".

authors: Swami, V., Hochstöger, S., Kargl, E., & Stieger, S.
title: Hangry in the field: An experience sampling study on the impact of hunger on anger, irritability, and affect
finding: Over 21 days, 64 adults reported more anger and irritability and less pleasure when they felt hungrier, even after accounting for factors like age, sex and trait anger.
strength: early: a single, fairly small experience-sampling study.

authors: Roskam, I., Raes, M.-E., & Mikolajczak, M.
title: Exhausted parents: Development and preliminary validation of the Parental Burnout Inventory
finding: Developed a 22-item Parental Burnout Inventory and found parental burnout to be related to, but distinct from, job burnout, parental stress and depression.
strength: moderate: early validation work that started a fast-growing field.

authors: Jamieson, J. P., Nock, M. K., & Mendes, W. B.
title: Mind over matter: Reappraising arousal improves cardiovascular and cognitive responses to stress
finding: People told to see their stress arousal as helpful showed healthier cardiovascular responses and less attention to negative information than control groups.
strength: moderate: replicated in several studies, with modest effects.
